carrosseis.titulo: Trotsky’s lover ended up painting the man who had him killed.
carrosseis.legenda:
Trotsky’s lover ended up painting the man who had him killed.

The story the university leaves off the feminist T-shirt.

At the university, Frida Kahlo is a “feminist icon.” Her life has chapters the print does not show. With dates:

• January 1937: Trotsky, exiled by Stalin, arrives in Mexico. Diego Rivera, Frida’s husband, secures the asylum, and the couple house him at the Blue House, in Coyoacán, with his wife, Natalia Sedova.
• 1937: Frida and Trotsky have an affair, under her husband’s roof, with Natalia in the house. The affair is over by July. On 7 November 1937, Frida gives Trotsky Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky.
• 1939: Rivera breaks with Trotsky, who leaves the Blue House.
• 20 August 1940: the Soviet agent Ramón Mercader attacks Trotsky in Coyoacán. He dies on the 21st.
• c. 1954: Frida, by then a Stalinist, paints Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick and Frida and Stalin. She dies on 13 July 1954.

The argument: Trotsky was killed in 1940 by an agent of Stalin’s secret police, on Stalin’s orders. In 1954, Frida painted Frida and Stalin, a portrait of devotion to the dictator. So Trotsky’s former lover ended up honoring the man who had him killed.

The T-shirt chooses the chapter. The whole story is in the dates.

Save this for when someone admires Frida, and send it to them.

#FridaKahlo #Trotsky #History

- Pavel Sudoplatov, Special Tasks (Little, Brown, 1994), pp. 69 and 71, on the operation against Trotsky.

carrosseis.titulo: Doctor: a boy raised as a girl, and it worked. In 2004, at 38, he killed himself.
carrosseis.legenda:
Doctor: a boy raised as a girl, and it worked. In 2004, at 38, he killed himself.

Bruce (later David) Reimer was born on 22 August 1965, in Canada, twin of Brian. In 1966 a botched circumcision destroyed his penis. The parents saw the sexologist John Money on television and took the boy to Johns Hopkins, in Baltimore. Money argued that boy or girl identity came from upbringing. At 22 months David was castrated and raised as “Brenda,” with dresses and hormones. Brian was the control.

In 1975 Money published the case as “Ablatio penis: normal male infant sex-reassigned as a girl,” and presented it as a success. At 14, the boy refused a girl’s identity, was told the truth, and chose the name David.

In 1997 Milton Diamond and Keith Sigmundson published the follow-up: David had never accepted being a girl. Brian died in 2002. David killed himself on 4 May 2004.

If sex were only upbringing, David would have accepted himself as a girl. He did not. So the case Money called a success shows the opposite.

Sources:
John Money, “Ablatio penis: normal male infant sex-reassigned as a girl,” Archives of Sexual Behavior (1975).
Milton Diamond and H. Keith Sigmundson, “Sex reassignment at birth: long-term review and clinical implications,” Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine (1997).
John Colapinto, As Nature Made Him (2000), for the later history up to that date. The death on 4 May 2004 is from contemporary reports of that year (and later accounts by Colapinto).

carrosseis.titulo: Picasso, the Communist Party painter, died a millionaire. His grandson drank bleach.
carrosseis.legenda:
Picasso, the Communist Party painter, died a millionaire. His grandson drank bleach.

Pablo Picasso died on 8 April 1973, at 91. A member of the French Communist Party from 1944, designer of the dove for the World Peace Congress (1949) and winner of the Lenin Peace Prize (1962), he left about 45,000 works and no will.

His grandson Pablito, 24, son of Paulo, the painter's first son, was refused entry, with Marina, when Picasso died. After that refusal he drank bleach (The New York Times, 17 April 1973). He was already in hospital on the funeral day, and died three months later. Marina wrote in 2001 that they grew up with little money and were often turned away at the gate of villa La Californie, in Cannes.

The obvious objection: Paulo was an adult, the widow barred him, and Marina is an interested party. But Paulo was chauffeur to his millionaire father, and the grandchildren's poverty lasted for decades while the grandfather lived.

The argument:
• Anyone who lends his name to the party of the poor, and leaves his own grandson in poverty when he could have lifted him out of it, denies at home what he signs on the poster.
• Picasso, a PCF member and a millionaire, left his grandchildren to grow up with little money (Marina Picasso, 2001).
• So Picasso denied at home what he signed on the poster.

Which counts for more: the dove on the poster, or the grandson at the gate?

Sources:
• Marina Picasso, Picasso, mon grand-père (Denoël, 2001); English, Picasso: My Grandfather, trans. Catherine Temerson (Riverhead, 2001).
• The New York Times, "Picasso Buried in a Private Rite," 17 April 1973.
• About 45,000 works and a six-year partition, settled in 1979, are standard in English estate reporting.

Images: Wikimedia Commons. Chapelle Notre-Dame-de-Vie de Mougins, Berdea (CC BY-SA 3.0); "20220503 141620 Villa La Californie," Indigo&fushia (CC BY-SA 4.0); "Pablo picasso 1," Vea y Lea (public domain); others in the public domain.

carrosseis.titulo: Whoever drives God out of society ends up worshipping a dictator. T. S. Eliot warned in 1939.
carrosseis.legenda:
Whoever drives God out of society ends up worshipping a dictator. T. S. Eliot warned in 1939.

Eliot, later the 1948 Nobel laureate in Literature, gave three lectures at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, in March 1939. Faber published them in October as The Idea of a Christian Society. He said the essay was not meant as an anti-communist or anti-fascist manifesto.

He did not trust a hollow democracy: “The term ‘democracy’ does not contain enough positive content to stand alone against the forces that you dislike; it can easily be transformed by them.” And the line that made the carousel travel: “If you will not have God (and He is a jealous God) you should pay your respects to Hitler or Stalin.”

The first premise comes from a secular sociologist. In The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912), Émile Durkheim wrote that a society cannot go on forever in the void left when the old gods grow old or die. In 1793, Paris raised an altar to Reason. When a society becomes enthusiastic about a man, Durkheim wrote, that man will be, as it were, deified. He died in 1917. He was describing the mechanism, not Hitler or Stalin.

In 1948, in Notes Towards the Definition of Culture, Eliot wrote that no culture has appeared or developed except together with a religion.

Sources:
T. S. Eliot, The Idea of a Christian Society (Faber and Faber, first edition, October 1939), pp. 13, 57 and 63.
T. S. Eliot, Notes Towards the Definition of Culture (1948), p. 13 (introduction).
Émile Durkheim, The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, trans. Joseph Ward Swain (Allen & Unwin, 1915), pp. 213-214 (Book II, ch. VII; the “old gods” sentence is in the conclusion). French original 1912.

carrosseis.titulo: You cannot understand the left without this word: infantilization.
carrosseis.legenda:
You cannot understand the left without this word: infantilization.

Lyle H. Rossiter Jr., a forensic psychiatrist who evaluated defendants for the courts, writes in The Liberal Mind (2006): Rossiter's point, in The Liberal Mind, is that as governments become more actively custodial, the governed become more passive and dependent. Custodial means treating the adult as a child.

The state, he says, is “a proper source from which to gratify the longings of the people for various forms of parental care.” And: “The modern state has taken on the role of an apparently benign, generous, omnipotent and god-like parent, who serves as custodian, manager, provider and caretaker, all to the detriment of the people.” In his account, “We have, in effect, parentified our governments.”

Under modern liberalism, the citizen “is not called to maturity but is instead invited to begin a second childhood.” The usual excuse is to blame “society.” Rossiter answers: “A competent individual always remains a unique and lifelong cause of his own experience.”

On character: “They do not feel entitled to be subsidized by persons with whom they have no prior personal relationship or contractual duty.”

No one learns to do what someone else always does for him. To keep an adult unable to do what is his to do is to infantilize him. The left calls it progress to hand the state, as a permanent right, what belongs to the adult. So that idea of progress infantilizes the adult. If you miss this, you do not understand the left.

I read this book 10 years ago, before it became fashionable.

Sources:
Lyle H. Rossiter Jr., The Liberal Mind: The Psychological Causes of Political Madness (2006). English wording from the author’s excerpts at libertymind.com. The custodial-governments sentence matches the Portuguese edition photographed for this series (Vide, 2016, p. 47).

Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II.

carrosseis.titulo: The left has a psychiatric report. The diagnosis: madness. Lyle Rossiter, a forensic psychiatrist, gave his book the subtitle “The Psychological Causes of Political Madness.”
carrosseis.legenda:
The left has a psychiatric report. The diagnosis: madness. Lyle Rossiter, a forensic psychiatrist, gave his book the subtitle “The Psychological Causes of Political Madness.”

He describes how a self-governing adult is formed. Under modern liberalism, he writes, the citizen “is not called to maturity but is instead invited to begin a second childhood.” The modern state has taken on the role of a “god-like parent.”

Among the early foundations he lists are tolerance for frustration, a reduction of infantile dependence, and the loss of the child’s sense that the world exists to serve him. Without an early limit, he argues, the urge to dominate overpowers respect for the sovereignty of others.

An honest warning: the book does not say that every spoiled child becomes a militant. It shows the mechanism. Those excused from effort are left without the virtues of self-reliance and self-control.

The argument: to demand that someone else provide what you can obtain by your own effort is the spoiled child’s conduct. The state produces nothing: what it gives, it first took from those who work. An able adult who asks the state for what he could earn acts like a spoiled child, with the state in the parents’ place.

I read this book 10 years ago, before it became fashionable.

Sources:
Lyle H. Rossiter Jr., The Liberal Mind: The Psychological Causes of Political Madness (2006). Author biography at libertymind.com: more than 2,700 civil and criminal cases. English wording from the author’s excerpts at libertymind.com (On the Ideals and Dangers of Liberalism; On the Appeal of Modern Liberalism). Lists from the early-childhood chapters are given as paraphrase; the English pages were not confirmed in a citable official source. carrosseis.titulo: The heir of the Frankfurt School admitted: human rights are a Jewish-Christian inheritance.
carrosseis.legenda:
The heir of the Frankfurt School admitted: human rights are a Jewish-Christian inheritance.

“To this day, there is no alternative to it,” Jürgen Habermas said in 1999, in a conversation with Eduardo Mendieta. Habermas (1929-2026) was the leading name of the second generation of the Frankfurt School.

The sentence, in English, is this: “Egalitarian universalism, from which sprang the ideas of freedom and social solidarity, of an autonomous conduct of life and emancipation, of the individual morality of conscience, human rights and democracy, is the direct heir to the Judaic ethic of justice and the Christian ethic of love.” He adds that, to this day, there is no alternative to that legacy, and that “everything else is just idle postmodern talk.”

He was speaking of historical origin, not calling for conversion. That is already enough to drop the myth that human rights were born against the biblical inheritance.

John Lennox, emeritus professor of mathematics at Oxford, quotes the same admission when answering the new atheists.

Sources:
Jürgen Habermas, "A Conversation About God and the World," interview by Eduardo Mendieta, 1999, in Time of Transitions (Polity, 2006), pp. 150-151.

carrosseis.titulo: Plato wrote that tyranny is born only from democracy.
carrosseis.legenda:
Plato wrote that tyranny is born only from democracy.

In Republic VIII, in Paul Shorey's translation (Plato in Twelve Volumes, Harvard / Heinemann, 1969), democracy falls by the good it pursues: a hunger for freedom, when the city is "intoxicated by drinking too deep of that unmixed wine" (562d). At 564a: "tyranny develops out of no other constitution than democracy: from the height of liberty, I take it, the fiercest extreme of servitude." The tyrant "sprouts from a protectorate root and from nothing else" (565d), after the demos puts forward "one man as its special champion and protector" (565c). In the early days he smiles, swears he is not a tyrant, cancels debts and divides land. Then he invents some war, so that the people will need a chief.

Aristotle, his pupil, checks it against history. In Politics 1310b, trans. H. Rackham (Harvard / Heinemann, 1944): "almost the greatest number of tyrants have risen, it may be said, from being demagogues, having won the people's confidence by slandering the notables." In old times, "whenever the same man became both leader of the people and general, they used to change the constitution to a tyranny" (1305a).

A conservative mistrusts the man who grows by accusing the notables and asking for power in the people's name.

Sources:
Plato, Republic VIII, 562b-d, 564a, 565c-566e, trans. Paul Shorey, Loeb, 1969.
Aristotle, Politics V, 1305a and 1310b, trans. H. Rackham, Loeb, 1944.

carrosseis.titulo: Stalin wanted a country without God. In the 1937 census, the majority declared themselves believers.
carrosseis.legenda:
Stalin wanted a country without God. In the 1937 census, the majority declared themselves believers.

On 6 January 1937, on the eve of the Orthodox Christmas, census takers knocked at every door. Atheism had been official doctrine for 20 years. Question no. 5 on the form, for those aged 16 or over, was a single word: religion.

Even so, 55.3 million people declared themselves believers, against 42.2 million non-believers: 56.7% of those who answered. Nearly 1 million refused to answer. The census counted about 162 million people, fewer than the regime expected, with the shortfall greater in Kazakhstan, Ukraine and southern Russia, regions hit by famine early in the decade.

The results were declared defective and shelved. Olimpiy Kvitkin and other officials were arrested. The purge reached Ivan Kraval, the head of Soviet statistics. The 1937 figures were published in Russia only in the 1990s.

After 20 years of official atheism, the majority still believed. The regime arrested those who counted.

Sources:
Felix Corley, "Believers' Responses to the 1937 and 1939 Soviet Censuses," Religion, State and Society 22, no. 4 (1994): question no. 5 ("religion"), age 16 or over, the date 6 January 1937 (Orthodox Christmas Eve), 55,277,049 believers, 42,243,214 non-believers, 890,869 refusals, and a total of some 162 million.
V. B. Zhiromskaya, I. N. Kiselev and Yu. A. Poliakov, Polveka pod grifom "sekretno" (Nauka, 1996); the same figures rounded as 55.3 million, 42.2 million, 56.7%, and 0.9 million refusals, and the greater shortfall in the famine regions.
Pravda, 26 September 1937, on the census being ruled defective.

carrosseis.titulo: Venezuela reached 94% poverty, with the largest oil reserve.
carrosseis.legenda:
Venezuela reached 94% poverty, with the largest oil reserve.

The poverty figure is from 2021; the reserve is from the OPEC yearbook. In the 2025 Statistical Yearbook, Venezuela’s proved reserve at the end of 2024 is 303.221 billion barrels, the largest among the members. Chávez governed from 2 February 1999 to 5 March 2013. After 2010, OPEC began listing Venezuela first in reserves.

The IMF, in 2019, estimated a 65% fall in GDP since 2013. ECLAC estimated 74% over the same stretch. The Central Bank of Venezuela, on 29 May 2019, published inflation of 130,060% in 2018 (and 862.6% in 2017). ENCOVI, a survey by universities in Caracas, put income poverty at 94.5% in 2021, and extreme poverty at 76.6%. The R4V platform, of the UN and its partners, has counted more than 6.9 million Venezuelans in host countries.

Hayek, in 1945, explained the problem of the central plan: knowledge is not concentrated in anyone, and prices coordinate what a single office cannot reach. They taught that extreme poverty is a lack of resources. Venezuela has the largest OPEC reserve and reached 94.5% poverty. So the collapse is not a lack of oil.

Sources:
OPEC, Statistical Yearbook 2025, proved reserves at end-2024.
OPEC, Annual Statistical Bulletin 2010/2011, Table 3.1, p. 22 (Venezuela first at end-2010: 296,501 million barrels, ahead of Saudi Arabia at 264,516).

carrosseis.titulo: The atheist Richard Dawkins replied in 2014 to someone who might have a child with Down syndrome: “Abort it and try again.”
carrosseis.legenda:
The atheist Richard Dawkins replied in 2014 to someone who might have a child with Down syndrome: “Abort it and try again.”

The tweet, on 20 August 2014, reads: “Abort it and try again. It would be immoral to bring it into the world if you have the choice.” A mother of a boy with Down syndrome answered, as reported by The Guardian and the BBC: “I would fight till my last breath for the life of my son. No dilemma.” The Down’s Syndrome Association said people with Down’s syndrome “can and do live full and rewarding lives.”

The next day, on his own site, Dawkins granted that his “phraseology may have been tactlessly vulnerable to misunderstanding,” but he did not retreat: if morality seeks to increase happiness and reduce suffering, giving birth in that case “might actually be immoral from the point of view of the child’s own welfare.”

In 1922, in Eugenics and Other Evils, G. K. Chesterton was already answering those who wanted science and the state to decide who should be born. The worth of a person comes from what he is, not from the happiness predicted for him.

Sources:
Richard Dawkins, tweet, 20 August 2014, as he quotes it in “Abortion & Down Syndrome: An Apology for Letting Slip the Dogs of Twitterwar,” richarddawkins.net, 21 August 2014 (Wayback Machine capture, 19 October 2014).

carrosseis.titulo: Marx wrote to a friend in mourning: it ought to have been my mother who died.
carrosseis.legenda:
Marx wrote to a friend in mourning: it ought to have been my mother who died.

On 7 January 1863, Engels told Marx that Mary Burns, his companion in Manchester, had died suddenly. “The poor girl loved me with all her heart.” The next day, Marx gave 2 sentences of condolence and a whole paragraph to his own debts: the butcher, the baker, the rent, the girls’ school fees. And he wrote: “Instead of Mary, ought it not to have been my mother, who is in any case a prey to physical ailments and has had her fair share of life?” He admitted: “It is dreadfully selfish of me.”

On 13 January, Engels wrote: “You thought it a fit moment to assert the superiority of your 'dispassionate turn of mind'.” To be fair: on 24 January Marx wrote that it was very wrong of him to write that letter, and on 26 January Engels sent £100.

Marx’s mother died in Trier on 30 November 1863. On 2 December he wrote that, circumstances being what they were, he “presumably, was needed more than my mater,” and: “I have got to go to Trier to settle the question of the legacy.” He asked Engels for the money for the journey.

Marx preached “to each according to his needs” (Critique of the Gotha Programme, 1875). In 1863, he measured his elderly mother by his own need. Burke, in 1790, said the opposite: public affection begins in the “little platoon” of each of us.

Sources:
Engels to Marx, 7 January 1863 (MECW 41, p. 441); Marx to Engels, 8 January 1863 (p. 442), 24 January 1863 (p. 444), 2 December 1863 (p. 495); Engels to Marx, 13 January 1863 (p. 443) and 26 January 1863 (p. 446). Marx and Engels, Collected Works, vol. 41; German: MEW 30, Dietz, 1964.
Karl Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875).

carrosseis.titulo: The book in which George Orwell unmasked communism was blocked in 1944: the publisher refused Animal Farm so as not to offend Stalin.
carrosseis.legenda:
The book in which George Orwell unmasked communism was blocked in 1944: the publisher refused Animal Farm so as not to offend Stalin.

Orwell finished Animal Farm at the end of 1943. In the preface “The Freedom of the Press,” he says the book was refused by 4 publishers, and only one of them on ideological grounds.

A publisher first accepted it, then consulted the Ministry of Information. Orwell quotes the letter: “the fable does follow, as I see now, so completely the progress of the Russian Soviets and their two dictators, that it can apply only to Russia,” and the choice of pigs as the ruling caste “will no doubt give offence to many people.”

On 13 July 1944, T. S. Eliot refused the book for Faber: “we have no conviction” that this was “the right point of view from which to criticise the political situation.”

Secker & Warburg published the book in August 1945. The preface on that censorship only came out in 1972.

Sources:
George Orwell, “The Freedom of the Press,” proposed preface to Animal Farm (1945), published in the Times Literary Supplement, 15 September 1972; text at The Orwell Foundation.

carrosseis.titulo: Fidel’s own daughter fled Cuba in a wig.
carrosseis.legenda:
Fidel’s own daughter fled Cuba in a wig.

Alina Fernández was born in Havana in 1956, from an affair of Fidel’s with Naty Revuelta. At 10 she learned who her father was. She never took the surname Castro, and she never called him “dad.” She had trips abroad denied, and of her father’s Cuba she said: “You felt you were living in a madhouse.”

On 19 December 1993 she left Havana with a Spanish woman’s passport, a wig, makeup, and extra weight so as not to be recognised, as El País reported on 24 December 1993. Her daughter, who had turned 16 the day before, stayed on the island. In Columbus, in the United States, Alina said: “I don't care whether his days are numbered or not, but the days I have left until I see my daughter again.”

To be fair: on 27 December, after the Reverend Jesse Jackson’s visit, Fidel said the granddaughter may leave if her father and grandmother agreed. Mother and daughter were reunited on 31 December 1993.

The Universal Declaration of 1948 (art. 13) says everyone may leave his own country. Alina had trips denied and left only in disguise. So not even Fidel’s daughter had that right. Fidel himself had given the rule in 1961: “Within the Revolution, everything; against the Revolution, nothing.”

carrosseis.titulo: In 1962, East Germany's communists left an 18-year-old to bleed for 50 minutes at the foot of the Wall.
carrosseis.legenda:
In 1962, East Germany's communists left an 18-year-old to bleed for 50 minutes at the foot of the Wall.

Peter Fechter, a bricklayer from East Berlin, tried to flee on 17 August 1962 near Checkpoint Charlie. His colleague, Helmut Kulbeik, made it across. Fechter was shot and fell on the Eastern side.

On the Western side, hundreds of people shouted “Murderers!” West Berlin police threw bandages over the Wall. After 50 minutes, when his cries had stopped, the guards carried him off behind a smoke screen laid on purpose (the Chronik der Mauer file says “künstlich gelegte Nebelwand”). His death was recorded at the People's Police hospital.

The shooters were tried in 1997. The autopsy used at the trial showed he could not have been saved even with immediate aid.

Share this. Fechter must not be forgotten. Like it, and save it.

carrosseis.titulo: Jane Fonda posed, smiling, on a cannon of communist Vietnam.
carrosseis.legenda:
Jane Fonda posed, smiling, on a cannon of communist Vietnam.

In July 1972 the United States was at war with North Vietnam. Shot-down American pilots were held prisoner in Hanoi. Months after the Oscar for Klute, Jane Fonda spent 2 weeks in the country and was photographed smiling, seated on a North Vietnamese anti-aircraft gun, the type of weapon used against American planes. The photo ran, among other papers, in The York Dispatch of 17 July 1972, p. 7.

On Radio Hanoi she spoke to American soldiers. In the transcript collected in the U.S. House hearings (Committee on Internal Security, Travel to Hostile Areas, HR 16742, 19 and 25 September 1972, p. 7671), she praised the militia women “who are so gentle and poetic, whose voices are so beautiful, but who, when American planes are bombing their city, become such good fighters.” The next year, Operation Homecoming brought the prisoners home.

Anyone who claims to be for peace and poses on the other side's weapon has already chosen a camp. The photo did the work of propaganda.

Like it, share it, and send it to someone who has only seen the activist, not the weapon.

The argument:
Anyone who claims to be for peace does not pose on the weapon of one side in a war. In July 1972, Fonda posed, smiling, on an anti-aircraft gun in Hanoi and spoke on the regime's radio. So the visit took the side of those who were firing at American planes.

carrosseis.legenda:
JFK's father had his 23-year-old daughter lobotomized, without telling her mother. Rosemary never spoke clearly again.

Rosemary Kennedy was born on 13 September 1918, in Brookline, Massachusetts. She had trouble learning from childhood. In 1938, with her father, Joseph Kennedy, ambassador to the United Kingdom, she was presented to King George VI and Queen Elizabeth.

Back in the United States in 1940 she became, in her sister Eunice's words, “increasingly irritable and difficult.” The doctors told her father that a lobotomy would calm the outbursts. Joseph Kennedy decided on the surgery and told his wife, Rose, only afterwards.

In November 1941, Walter Freeman and James Watts operated on Rosemary. Watts told Ronald Kessler: “We went through the top of the head.” He thought she was awake; while they cut, Freeman asked her questions. When she grew incoherent, they stopped.

The surgery left her without clear speech. She spent the rest of her life in institutions. According to The Independent, her mother went some 20 years without visiting her. The lobotomy became public only in 1987, in a book by Doris Kearns Goodwin. Rosemary died on 7 January 2005, at 86.

In 1949 the Nobel Prize in Medicine honoured Egas Moniz, the inventor of lobotomy. The book on the shelf is G. K. Chesterton's Eugenics and Other Evils.

Sources:
Ronald Kessler, Sins of the Father: Joseph P. Kennedy and the Dynasty He Founded, 1996, p. 243.

carrosseis.titulo: 7 books that open the leftist mind from the inside.
carrosseis.legenda:
7 books that open the leftist mind from the inside.

Fools, Frauds and Firebrands. Roger Scruton, 2015. Portraits of the New Left: the theory loses the concrete person, and the system is what remains.
The Uses of Pessimism. Roger Scruton, 2010. The mind that is going to save history sells the best-case story and calls desire a science.
The Gods of Revolution. Christopher Dawson, 1972. The French Revolution worked as a political religion, with dogma, feast days and heretics.
How to Be a Conservative. Roger Scruton, 2014. The mind that remakes society from a theory ignores the agreement that already holds us up.
Reflections on the Revolution in France. Edmund Burke, 1790. The abstract mind tears up the institution and calls that a right. The bill arrives armed.
Intellectuals. Paul Johnson, 1988. The intellectual preaches humanity and does not keep the rule in his own house.
The Opium of the Intellectuals. Raymond Aron, 1955. The intellectual makes an opium of communism and does not want to live under the regime he praises.

Seven books, not ten. Each line has to fit the work. What had no clean jacket was left out.

carrosseis.titulo: 7 books show why socialism never works.
carrosseis.legenda:
7 books show why socialism never works.

Marxism Unmasked. Ludwig von Mises, lectures of 1952. Class logic replaces a single logic, and there is no calculation without prices.
Socialism. Ludwig von Mises, 1922. Without private property in the means of production there is no price. Without a price, the plan cannot calculate.
The Fatal Conceit. F. A. Hayek, 1988. The fatal conceit is to think one mind can design the order that no one planned as a whole.
Omnipotent Government. Ludwig von Mises, 1944. The state that can do everything does not stay in the economy. Statism marches toward conflict.
Karl Marx and the Close of His System. Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk, 1896. Marx's theory of value fails in the passage from value to the price of production.
The Open Society and Its Enemies. Karl Popper, 1945, volume 2. Hegel and Marx enter as enemies of the open society: history has no party script.
The Road to Serfdom. F. A. Hayek, 1944. Central planning gathers power in one centre. From that centre comes serfdom, not a freedom agreed together.

Seven books, not ten. Each line has to fit the work. What had no clean jacket was left out.

carrosseis.titulo: How did Fidel ration food?
carrosseis.legenda:
How did Fidel ration food?

On 12 March 1962, a decree of the revolutionary government created the “libreta de abastecimiento,” the ration book. It fixes how much each person may buy of each product. Each purchase is written down at the bodega, the state's neighbourhood grocery. Over the years it came to include cigarettes, matches, cooking gas, even light bulbs.

On 6 June 1962, residents of Cárdenas protested by banging empty pots (the Protesta de las Calderas). To administer the book, the state created OFICODA, which issues each citizen's book every year.

In June 2026, Díaz-Canel said the “almost disappeared basic basket” would be guaranteed only to pensioners, families with chronically ill children, and the vulnerable. In October 2026, AFP found Havana bodegas closed or replaced; in recent days Cubans could not buy anything with the book. No national rule has abolished it.

The argument: if Cuban socialism guaranteed food for everyone, the ration-book basket would not be “almost gone.” In June 2026, Díaz-Canel himself spoke of the “almost disappeared basic basket.” So Cuban socialism does not guarantee food for everyone. The regime itself is the one saying so.

In the Grand Inquisitor, Dostoevsky has men laying their freedom at the feet of power: “Make us your slaves, but feed us” (Constance Garnett, The Brothers Karamazov).

Share this with someone who thinks that, in Cuba, socialism guarantees food.

carrosseis.titulo: The socialist pastor Jim Jones led 909 people to their deaths and called it “revolutionary suicide.”
carrosseis.legenda:
The socialist pastor Jim Jones led 909 people to their deaths and called it “revolutionary suicide.”

Jim Jones founded the Peoples Temple in Indianapolis in 1955, and preached what he called “apostolic socialism.” In 1977 he took hundreds of followers to a commune in Guyana. On FBI tape Q 50 he said he believed they were “the purest communists there are.”

On 18 November 1978, Temple gunmen killed U.S. Congressman Leo Ryan, three journalists and a defector on the Port Kaituma airstrip. That same night, in Jonestown, Jones said into the microphone: “This is a revolutionary suicide. This is not a self-destructive suicide.”

On the same tape he said: “This is not the way for people who are Socialists or Communists to die. We must die with some dignity.” At Jonestown, 909 people died, 304 of them children. At least 70 were injected with the poison. With Port Kaituma and Georgetown, the total was 918.

Killing innocents is murder, whatever name the cause is given. The book on the shelf is James Billington's Fire in the Minds of Men, on the origins of the faith that revolution saves.

Share this with someone who thinks a fine cause justifies any means.

carrosseis.titulo: Sartre and Beauvoir defended 3 men accused of sex with minors under 15.
carrosseis.legenda:
Sartre and Beauvoir defended 3 men accused of sex with minors under 15.

Le Monde, 26 January 1977, “À propos d’un procès.” Dejager, Gallien and Burckhardt, arrested in the autumn of 1973, were going before a jury accused of “indecent assault without violence” against minors under 15.

• Their version: “3 years in prison for caresses and kisses is quite enough.”

• The same text states the charge they risked: “for having had sexual relations with these minors, boys and girls,” or “for having encouraged and photographed their sexual games.”

• The argument: the children “consented,” although the law denied them “any right to consent.”

• In parentheses: “If a 13-year-old girl has a right to the pill, what is it for?”

• 69 signatories, among them Aragon, Barthes, Deleuze, Guattari, Glucksmann, Lyotard, Sollers, Kouchner and Jack Lang. Foucault did not sign this one; he and Derrida are on the letter of May 1977.

• Gabriel Matzneff also signed. In 2020, Vanessa Springora, in Consent, told of the relationship she had with him from the age of 14, when he was 50.

The argument:
Anyone who signs a text that uses the “consent” of minors to defend men accused of sex with them maintains, in writing, that a minor can consent to sex.
The 69 signatories signed a text that defends the 3 by saying the children, under 15, “consented,” and objects that the law denies them “any right to consent.”
So those who signed for the liberty of the 3 accused maintained, in writing, that minors under 15 can consent to sex.

carrosseis.titulo: The New Atheists do not merely want to stop believing. They want to rid the world of religion.
carrosseis.legenda:
The New Atheists do not merely want to stop believing. They want to rid the world of religion.

The Oxford mathematician John Lennox sums up their agenda in three sentences:

1. Religion is a dangerous delusion: it leads to violence and war.
2. We must therefore get rid of religion: science will achieve that.
3. We do not need God to be good: atheism can provide a perfectly adequate base for ethics.

Notice the “therefore.” If religion is a threat, the next step is to remove it.

That is why Lennox says they “are perhaps better described as anti-theists,” unlike the atheist who does not believe in God herself but is quite happy for others to believe, provided they do not disturb her.

The OED, as cited by Lennox: atheism is “disbelief in or denial of the existence of a God.” Shaftesbury, 1709: “To believe nothing of a designing Principle or Mind, nor any Cause, Measure or Rule of things but Chance… is to be a perfect atheist.”

Unbelief is an opinion. Eradication is a programme.

Share this with someone who thinks the New Atheism is only “not believing.”

Sources:

carrosseis.titulo: Foucault argued on the radio for ending the age of consent.
carrosseis.legenda:
Foucault argued on the radio for ending the age of consent.

On 4 April 1978, on France Culture, Michel Foucault debated Guy Hocquenghem and Jean Danet on the age of consent in French criminal law. He said: “An age barrier laid down by law does not have much sense. Again, the child may be trusted to say whether or not he was subjected to violence.” The transcript appeared in Recherches no. 37 (1979) and in Dits et écrits III, text 263.

In May 1977 he had already signed a letter to the commission for the revision of the Penal Code asking for that rule to be changed. A law with a fixed age already allows the child to be heard; removing the age removes the barrier the adult may not cross.

The critic of power, an icon of the university, argued on the radio for taking from the child the legal barrier of age.

Like it, share it, and send it to someone who takes this lecture into the university.

The argument:
Anyone who denounces the power of the strong does not take away the law that protects the weak. In 1978, on the radio, Foucault said that a fixed age “does not have much sense.” So he argued for removing that barrier from the child.

carrosseis.titulo: You cannot understand the left if you do not know this word: hegemony.
carrosseis.legenda:
You cannot understand the left if you do not know this word: hegemony.

Hegemony, in Gramsci's Notebooks, is not only government. In Notebook 12, §1, the standard English (Hoare and Nowell-Smith, Selections from the Prison Notebooks, p. 12; Gerratana vol. 3, p. 1519) reads: the intellectuals are the dominant group's “deputies” exercising the subaltern functions of social hegemony and political government. The same page sets out the consent of the masses, with the coercive apparatus held in reserve.

In practice, the press, the school and culture repeat the same direction, and the new course looks like common sense. The conservative reply is that inherited common sense is not a piece of propaganda.

The argument:
They taught that culture is only taste, not power.
In Notebook 12, hegemony is direction by consent, with coercion held in reserve.
So the lecture hides an instrument of power.

Does that account hold in the conversation in your own house?

carrosseis.titulo: Marx asked whether the wage creates property for the worker. His answer: “Not a bit.”
carrosseis.legenda:
Marx asked whether the wage creates property for the worker. His answer: “Not a bit.”

In ch. II of the Manifesto of the Communist Party (1848), Marx and Engels sum up communist theory in one phrase: “Abolition of private property.” And they ask (Moore, 1888): “But does wage-labour create any property for the labourer? Not a bit. It creates capital.” The average wage, according to the text, only keeps the worker alive as a worker.

A century and a half earlier, John Locke had written that “the labour of his body, and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his” (Second Treatise, §27). In 1891 the encyclical Rerum Novarum said the opposite of Marx: if a man lives sparingly, saves, and invests his savings in land, “the land, in such case, is only his wages under another form” (official English of Rerum Novarum, n. 5, at vatican.va).

The argument:
1. If the wage never creates property, no worker buys a house with a saved wage.
2. Workers do buy houses with saved wages: in England, since 1775, in building societies.
So: Marx was wrong: the wage does create property for the worker.

The best Marxist objection: in the Manifesto, “property” is the capital that exploits other people's labour, and a house is not capital. The reply: the text's question is whether the wage creates property “for him,” and the same chapter says the average wage only replaces bare existence. A house paid off is not bare existence. And a house that is let becomes rent, that is, the capital the text says the worker will never have.

How many workers' houses refute the “Not a bit”?

Sources:
K. Marx and F. Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party, ch. II, Samuel Moore's English of 1888 (as on marxists.org).
John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689), §27.
Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum (15 May 1891), n. 5, official English at vatican.va.

carrosseis.titulo: Arthur Miller, Marilyn's ex, hid his son with Down syndrome.
carrosseis.legenda:
Arthur Miller, Marilyn's ex, hid his son with Down syndrome.

Miller was the playwright of the American left: the author of Death of a Salesman, he refused in 1956 to give names to the congressional committee, and he married Marilyn Monroe.

In November 1966 Daniel was born, his son with the photographer Inge Morath. The next day Miller told a friend the baby “wasn't right.” Within a few days Daniel was sent to a home for infants; at 4, to Southbury, 10 minutes from the house. Inge went almost every Sunday. Arthur, according to a friend, never wanted to see him.

To be fair: doctors still told parents to institutionalise, and 6 weeks before dying, in 2005, Miller made Daniel an heir equal to the other 3 children.

The argument:
• In the 1949 play, Linda says that “attention must be paid” to a forgotten man.
• In the 1987 autobiography, the son does not appear.
• So Miller did not pay attention to his son.
Inge saw what he avoided: the place looked “like a Hieronymus Bosch painting.”

What is compassion on the stage worth, if it is missing at home?

Suzanna Andrews, “Arthur Miller's Missing Act,” Vanity Fair, September 2007.
NPR, “Arthur Miller's Secret Son,” interview with Suzanna Andrews, 2007.

carrosseis.titulo: Soviet communists locked critics of the Party in a psychiatric hospital.
carrosseis.legenda:
Soviet communists locked critics of the Party in a psychiatric hospital.

In the 1960s Andrei Snezhnevsky's school created “sluggish schizophrenia,” with relatively mild symptoms. It was the diagnosis most used against dissidents.

Petro Grigorenko, a Red Army general, began in 1961 to criticise publicly the privileges of the Party elite. Arrested in 1964, he was examined at the Serbsky Institute in Moscow: a “paranoid development of the personality,” with “reformist ideas” among the symptoms.

In 1969, arrested in Tashkent, local experts found no illness. The KGB took him back to the Serbsky, which repeated the report. He remained interned until 26 June 1974.

The psychiatrist Semyon Gluzman, who in 1971 declared him sane, later served 7 years in a labour camp. In October 1991 a commission of psychiatrists reversed the diagnosis. Grigorenko had died in 1987, in New York.

The argument: a report that treats political ideas as a symptom is judging an opinion, not an illness. The Serbsky report of 1964 gave as a symptom of the general his “reformist ideas.” So the 1964 report judged an opinion, not an illness.

Share this with someone who thinks Soviet psychiatry was only medicine.

carrosseis.titulo: You cannot understand the left if you do not know this word: ressentiment.
carrosseis.legenda:
You cannot understand the left if you do not know this word: ressentiment.

In On the Genealogy of Morals (1887), First Essay, §10, Nietzsche describes, in Horace B. Samuel's 1913 English, “the revolt of the slaves in morals” that begins in “resentment becoming creative and giving birth to values.” Samuel renders Nietzsche's ressentiment as “resentment”; the headword of this piece remains ressentiment.

In ordinary life, the neighbour's success becomes proof of guilt. Justice is not born of rancour dressed as virtue.

The argument:
They taught that every moral revolt is justice.
In §10, “resentment becoming creative and giving birth to values,” by reaction. The headword is Nietzsche's ressentiment.
So not every morality of protest proves justice.

Does that account hold in the conversation in your own house?

carrosseis.titulo: Democracy can silence you without jailing anyone.
carrosseis.legenda:
Democracy can silence you without jailing anyone.

In 1835, Tocqueville called "impious and detestable" the maxim that a majority "has the right to do everything." Above it he placed justice: whoever refuses an unjust law appeals from the sovereignty of the people "to the sovereignty of the human race."

In the United States he visited, every door led to the majority. Public opinion formed it, the legislature obeyed it, the jury was the majority clothed with the right to try cases. In Baltimore, in 1812, a mob smashed an anti-war newspaper's presses and later killed General James Lingan in the jail; the jury acquitted the guilty.

The greater control was without violence: the majority "raises formidable barriers around the liberty of opinion." Outside them a writer need not fear an auto-da-fe, but "continued obloquy and persecution." The new master says you are free to think differently, but "you are henceforth a stranger among your people."

The argument:
1. Anyone who has no one to appeal to against a power has no guarantee against the tyranny of that power.
2. In the America of 1835, the minority had no one to appeal to against the majority.
So the minority had no guarantee against the tyranny of the majority.

The objection: social exclusion is not political power. Tocqueville answers that when legislature, jury and opinion obey the same majority, the border disappears: to whom does the excluded person appeal? If a man with total power abuses it, why would a majority not?

Send this to someone who thinks the majority is always right. Save it.

Sources: Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835), part 2, ch. 7 (Lawrence; Reeve for the jury, the barriers around opinion, and the stranger among your people). Baltimore, 1812: National Park Service; pamphlet of 1 September 1812. (Tocqueville's note spoke of "one of the journalists"; the man who died was General Lingan.)
Images: Chasseriau, Tocqueville, 1850; Hall of Representatives, 1832, NYPL (public domain).

carrosseis.titulo: In 1920, Margaret Sanger, a pioneer of birth control, wrote: "The most immoral practice of the day is breeding too many children."
carrosseis.legenda:
In 1920, Margaret Sanger, a pioneer of birth control, wrote: "The most immoral practice of the day is breeding too many children."

The sentence is in chapter 5 of Woman and the New Race (1920), in a chapter titled "The Wickedness of Creating Large Families." There she also called the encouragement of large families "the most serious evil of our times."

In the same chapter, on infant mortality, she wrote: "The most merciful thing that the large family does to one of its infant members is to kill it." And, in chapter 18, that birth control is "nothing more or less than the facilitation of the process of weeding out the unfit, of preventing the birth of defectives or of those who will become defectives."

In 1938, in the autobiography (p. 366), she herself recorded: "I accepted an invitation to talk to the women's branch of the Ku Klux Klan at Silver Lake, New Jersey." The book does not give the year. She later received "a dozen invitations" from similar groups. That does not prove she agreed with them, and we do not say that.

The argument is simple: a person's dignity does not depend on the usefulness someone else assigns to her, so no one has the authority to decide which people may be born. The book to read is Eugenics and Other Evils, by G. K. Chesterton, written in 1922 against eugenics.

Share this with someone who thinks eugenics stayed only in Germany. Like and save.

carrosseis.titulo: An atheist biologist called religious belief a useful illusion and fell into his own trap.
carrosseis.legenda:
An atheist biologist called religious belief a useful illusion and fell into his own trap.

David Sloan Wilson, in Darwin's Cathedral (2002), explains religion as an adaptation: it survives because it unites and motivates groups, not because it is true. And he offers a criterion: "Adaptation is the gold standard against which rationality must be judged, along with all other forms of thought."

Alvin Plantinga quotes the whole passage in Where the Conflict Really Lies and shows the hidden premise: the theory already assumes that the belief is not aimed at truth.

And the crack: if adaptation judges all thought, Wilson's own theory would count only for being useful. But the same Wilson wrote in 2022 that science "worships factual realism as its God." The criterion knocks itself down.

Send this to someone who thinks religious belief is only a useful illusion. Save it so you can answer with the page in your hand.

Sources:

carrosseis.titulo: In 2004, the atheist philosopher Antony Flew left atheism because reason led him to DNA.
carrosseis.legenda:
In 2004, the atheist philosopher Antony Flew left atheism because reason led him to DNA.

In February 1985, Antony Flew met the philosopher Gary Habermas in Dallas. In May the two debated the resurrection of Jesus at Liberty University. The text that introduces the interview calls Flew arguably the world's foremost philosophical atheist.

They talked again in April 2000 and January 2003. Soon after the last meeting, Flew said by phone that he was considering becoming a theist. He did not change then. In January 2004 he said that he had: he had to go where the evidence leads.

The reason, in his words, was that the findings of more than fifty years of DNA research have provided materials for a new and enormously powerful argument to Design. He also recalls that Darwin started from a being that already reproduced.

Flew did not become a Christian. He accepts the label of deist, speaks of an Aristotelian God, with power and intelligence, and says: "I don't believe in the God of any revelatory system, although I am open to that." The interview was held early in 2004 and modified by both men through the year.

The argument: if atheism were always the position of reason, no one would leave it by following the evidence. Flew left, saying exactly that. The book to read is The Existence of God, by Richard Swinburne.

Share this with someone who thinks atheism is always the position of reason. Like and save.

Sources:
Gary R. Habermas and Antony Flew, My Pilgrimage from Atheism to Theism, Philosophia Christi, 2004: https://www.epsociety.org/articles/my-pilgrimage-from-atheism-to-theism/

carrosseis.titulo: In 1794, the French Revolution guillotined 16 Carmelites for keeping the religious life.
carrosseis.legenda:
In 1794, the French Revolution guillotined 16 Carmelites for keeping the religious life.

On 17 July 1794, in Paris, 16 women of the Carmel of Compiegne were executed: 11 choir nuns, 3 lay sisters and 2 servants of the convent. The Revolution had already closed the convents, and the charge was that they had remained in the religious life.

The guillotine stood in the Place du Trone Renverse, the square of the Overturned Throne, today Place de la Nation. According to witnesses, they sang on the way and at the foot of the scaffold. The youngest went first; the prioress went last, singing the "Laudate Dominum."

Ten days later, Robespierre was guillotined. The Carmelites lie in the common pit at Picpus. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1908) gives 1,298 victims of the Revolution in that pit; later standard counts often give 1,306. They were beatified in 1906.

The argument: a regime that executes people for keeping the religious life is not tolerant. The Revolution executed 16 Carmelites for that. So, on this point, it was not a victory of tolerance.

The book to read is Reflections on the Revolution in France, by Edmund Burke. Share, like, and save.

Sources:
William Bush, To Quell the Terror: The Mystery of the Vocation of the Sixteen Carmelites of Compiegne, ICS, 1999
"Martyrs of Compiegne", Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 4, 1908
Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790

carrosseis.titulo: Freud called hysterical the 14-year-old girl who felt disgust at a forced kiss.
carrosseis.legenda:
Freud called hysterical the 14-year-old girl who felt disgust at a forced kiss.

In 1900, an 18-year-old young woman, known in the literature as Dora (the case name of Ida Bauer), began treatment with Freud. By his own account, the treatment lasted no more than three months. The case was published in 1905.

At 14, Freud writes, she was seized by a family friend, Herr K., who kissed her on the mouth. Dora felt "a violent feeling of disgust," tore herself free and ran. Freud himself says the episode was "even better calculated to act as a sexual trauma."

Even so, he writes that the behaviour of this "child of fourteen" was already "entirely and completely hysterical." His rule: he would "without question consider a person hysterical" in whom an occasion for sexual excitement elicited feelings that were "preponderantly or exclusively unpleasurable." When Dora broke off the treatment, Freud called the gesture "an unmistakable act of vengeance."

So disgust in the face of what is wrong is not a symptom: it is a right reaction. The book to read is Sexual Desire, by Roger Scruton, who regards Freud's theory of the libido as incoherent.

Share this with someone who thinks psychoanalysis always listened to the victim. Like and save.

Sources:
Sigmund Freud, Fragment of an Analysis of a Case of Hysteria (1905), Penguin Freud Library vol. 8, pp. 58-59 and 150-151 (standard Strachey English).
Roger Scruton, Sexual Desire (1986); review in The Spectator, 1 March 1986.

carrosseis.titulo: Mussolini wrote: in fascism, nothing exists outside the State.
carrosseis.legenda:
Mussolini wrote: in fascism, nothing exists outside the State.

In the Enciclopedia Italiana, in 1932, he signed The Doctrine of Fascism: for the Fascist, everything is in the State, and nothing human or spiritual exists, much less has value, outside the State. In this sense Fascism is totalitarian. In the same doctrine he confessed that, of doctrine, he brought the experience of one only: that of socialism, from 1903-04 to the winter of 1914.

Before that, from 1912 to 1914, Mussolini edited Avanti!, the daily of the Italian Socialist Party. Circulation rose from 20,000 to about 100,000 copies. On 15 November 1914 he launched Il Popolo d'Italia, still with the banner "Quotidiano socialista." On 24 November the party expelled him. The banner stayed until 1 August 1918.

The doctrine also attacks the socialism of the class struggle, and democracy. What remains, on the paper he signed, is the State as the absolute. They taught fascism as simple "far right," the opposite of socialism. His text and his origin do not fit that lesson.

Like, share, and send it to someone who has only heard the classroom version.

The argument:
They taught that fascism is the opposite of socialism. Mussolini came from socialism and defined fascism as the absolute State. So the lesson hides both the origin and the text he signed.

Sources:
Benito Mussolini, "La dottrina del fascismo", Enciclopedia Italiana, 1932 (it.wikisource): Idee fondamentali VII; Dottrina politica I, IX and XI.
Dates for Avanti!, Il Popolo d'Italia and the expulsion: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, entry Mussolini (Emilio Gentile).

carrosseis.titulo: The "Jane Roe" of the case that legalized abortion in the US had the baby.
carrosseis.legenda:
The "Jane Roe" of the case that legalized abortion in the US had the baby.

In 1973, the Supreme Court struck down the state laws that banned abortion in Roe v. Wade. "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, 21, pregnant for the third time. Advised by friends, she said she had been raped, and later admitted it was an invention. The lawyers Linda Coffee and Sarah Weddington were looking for pregnant women who wanted an abortion, to take the case to court. She never attended a hearing of the case. The daughter was born during the case and was placed for adoption.

In 1995 she switched sides and called the case "the biggest mistake of my life." In a 2020 documentary she said even that activism was paid. So, on both sides, Jane Roe was used as a name.

The argument: if the decision had given Norma the abortion she was asking for, she would not have had the baby. Norma had the baby during the case, before the 1973 decision. So the decision did not give Norma the abortion she was asking for.

The book to read is On Human Nature, by Roger Scruton: a person is an end, never only a means.

Share this with someone who thinks Roe v. Wade was Jane Roe's victory. Like and save.

Sources:
Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 113 (1973).
Joshua Prager, The Family Roe (2021); the documentary AKA Jane Roe (2020).
Roger Scruton, On Human Nature (Princeton, 2017).

carrosseis.titulo: The Marxist Gramsci wrote: "I hate the indifferent." And said he would not waste his pity on them.
carrosseis.legenda:
The Marxist Gramsci wrote: "I hate the indifferent." And said he would not waste his pity on them.

On 11 February 1917, in Turin, Antonio Gramsci, then a young socialist, opened the single issue of La Citta futura with the text "Indifferenti." In 1921 he would help found the Italian Communist Party.

Quoting the poet Hebbel, he wrote that "to live means to be a partisan." Indifference "is abulia, it is parasitism, it is cowardice, it is not life." He calls each indifferent person to account for what he has done, "and especially for what he has not done." And he adds: "I feel that I can be inexorable, that I must not waste my pity." He closes: "I live, I am a partisan. That is why I hate whoever does not take a side, I hate the indifferent."

In the same issue, in "Discipline and Freedom," whoever does not follow a political discipline is "matter in a gaseous state," "hence useless and harmful."

The argument: every free adherence can be refused without fault. For Gramsci, joining the movement is "an act of independence and of liberation": a free adherence. So refusing that adherence is not a fault. The hatred of the indifferent does not stand even on his own premise.

Against the French Revolution, Edmund Burke defended prudence and inherited institutions. The book to read is Reflections on the Revolution in France.

Share this with someone who quotes "I hate the indifferent" without reading the rest. And save it.

Sources:
A. Gramsci, "Indifferenti" and "Disciplina e liberta", La Citta futura, single issue, Turin, 11 February 1917 (marxists.org/italiano/gramsci/17/cittafutura.htm).
Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790.

carrosseis.titulo: In 1920, Alexandra Kollontai wrote that "the state does not need the family." In 1936, the same State began to exalt the family.
carrosseis.legenda:
In 1920, Alexandra Kollontai wrote that "the state does not need the family." In 1936, the same State began to exalt the family.

Kollontai was the first woman in the Soviet government and People's Commissar for Social Welfare in 1917-18. In 1920 she published "Communism and the Family."

In it she says that the family "is ceasing to be necessary either to its members or to the nation as a whole," because the domestic economy "is no longer profitable." She also writes that the workers' state would come to replace the family, and that there would be only "our children, the children of Russia's communist workers."

In 1936 the USSR banned abortion and began to exalt the family and motherhood. The historian Wendy Goldman calls this phase "the resurrection of the family."

The argument is simple: anyone who can really dispense with an institution has no reason to restore it. The State that declared the family dispensable restored it 16 years later. The book to read is Conservatism, by Roger Scruton.

Save this for the next time they say the State cares for the family better than the family does. Share and like.

Sources:
A. Kollontai, "Communism and the Family" (1920), marxists.org/archive/kollonta/1920/communism-family.htm
W. Z. Goldman, Women, the State and Revolution, Cambridge University Press, 1993, ch. 8, pp. 296-336.
P. A. Michaels, "Motherhood, Patriotism, and Ethnicity: Soviet Kazakhstan and the 1936 Abortion Ban", Feminist Studies, 2001.
